title: The Money That Worked While Afia Slept

pages.text: Twelve-year-old Afia loved numbers the way musicians love rhythm. One Saturday afternoon in Ho, her nineteen-year-old brother Bra Yao counted out 1,000 Ghana cedis he had saved from building school desks and wardrobes. ‘I do not need to buy my big workshop saw for another three years,’ Bra Yao said. ‘I will just lock this 1,000 cedis inside my wooden cash box under the bed until then.’
sentences: Twelve-year-old Afia loved numbers the way musicians love rhythm.
One Saturday afternoon in Ho, her nineteen-year-old brother Bra Yao counted out 1,000 Ghana cedis he had saved from building school desks and wardrobes.
‘I do not need to buy my big workshop saw for another three years,’ Bra Yao said.
‘I will just lock this 1,000 cedis inside my wooden cash box under the bed until then.’
pages.alt: In their family living room in Ho, nineteen-year-old Bra Yao holds 1,000 cedis beside a wooden cash box while twelve-year-old Afia looks thoughtful.

pages.text: Just then, Auntie Akua, who worked at a licensed bank in town, stopped by after market. ‘Yao, keeping emergency cash safe is wise,’ she said, ‘but if 1,000 cedis sleeps inside a wooden box for three years, it faces a silent thief called inflation.’ Afia raised her eyebrows. ‘How can money be stolen if the box stays locked?’ she asked.
sentences: Just then, Auntie Akua, who worked at a licensed bank in town, stopped by after market.
‘Yao, keeping emergency cash safe is wise,’ she said, ‘but if 1,000 cedis sleeps inside a wooden box for three years, it faces a silent thief called inflation.’ Afia raised her eyebrows.
‘How can money be stolen if the box stays locked?’ she asked.
pages.alt: Auntie Akua in a blue blazer explains inflation to Afia and Bra Yao around the dining table.

pages.text: ‘Inflation is the general rise in the prices of goods and services over time,’ Auntie Akua explained. ‘Suppose a carpentry toolset costs 1,000 cedis today, and general prices rise by 8 percent over the next year: that same toolset will cost 1,080 cedis next year! Your cash box still holds 1,000 cedis, so its purchasing power, what the money can actually buy, has shrunk. To protect and grow long-term savings, your money must work while you sleep!’
sentences: ‘Inflation is the general rise in the prices of goods and services over time,’ Auntie Akua explained.
‘Suppose a carpentry toolset costs 1,000 cedis today, and general prices rise by 8 percent over the next year: that same toolset will cost 1,080 cedis next year!
Your cash box still holds 1,000 cedis, so its purchasing power, what the money can actually buy, has shrunk.
To protect and grow long-term savings, your money must work while you sleep!’
pages.alt: Afia draws a balance scale in her notebook showing a 1,000-cedi note weighed against a toolset whose price rises over time.

pages.text: Auntie Akua drew two columns in Afia’s exercise book. ‘First, let us compare simple interest and compound interest using an easy illustrative rate of 10 percent per year on your 1,000 cedis of principal,’ she said. ‘At the end of Year 1, 10 percent of 1,000 cedis is 100 cedis of interest. So whether you use simple or compound interest, your balance after one year is 1,000 plus 100 equals 1,100 cedis.’
sentences: Auntie Akua drew two columns in Afia’s exercise book.
‘First, let us compare simple interest and compound interest using an easy illustrative rate of 10 percent per year on your 1,000 cedis of principal,’ she said.
‘At the end of Year 1, 10 percent of 1,000 cedis is 100 cedis of interest.
So whether you use simple or compound interest, your balance after one year is 1,000 plus 100 equals 1,100 cedis.’
pages.alt: Auntie Akua and Afia calculate Year 1 interest (1,000 + 100 = 1,100 cedis) on a pad of grid paper.

pages.text: ‘Look what happens in Year 2 if you leave that 100 cedis of interest inside the account to compound,’ Afia said, her pencil flying! ‘In Year 2, you earn 10 percent not just on the original 1,000 cedis, but on the whole 1,100 cedis! Ten percent of 1,100 is 110 cedis. So 1,100 plus 110 equals 1,210 cedis, 10 cedis more than simple interest, because your first year’s interest earned its own interest!’
sentences: ‘Look what happens in Year 2 if you leave that 100 cedis of interest inside the account to compound,’ Afia said, her pencil flying!
‘In Year 2, you earn 10 percent not just on the original 1,000 cedis, but on the whole 1,100 cedis!
Ten percent of 1,100 is 110 cedis.
So 1,100 plus 110 equals 1,210 cedis, 10 cedis more than simple interest, because your first year’s interest earned its own interest!’
pages.alt: Afia points excitedly to the Year 2 bar showing an extra golden block of interest-on-interest on top of the stack.

pages.text: ‘Now calculate Year 3!’ challenged Bra Yao. Afia multiplied carefully: ‘Ten percent of 1,210 cedis is 121 cedis. Adding 121 to 1,210 gives 1,331 cedis at the end of Year 3! With simple interest, three years of 100 cedis would only be 1,300 cedis, so compounding created an extra 31 cedis without you lifting a hammer while you slept!’
sentences: ‘Now calculate Year 3!’ challenged Bra Yao.
Afia multiplied carefully: ‘Ten percent of 1,210 cedis is 121 cedis.
Adding 121 to 1,210 gives 1,331 cedis at the end of Year 3!
With simple interest, three years of 100 cedis would only be 1,300 cedis, so compounding created an extra 31 cedis without you lifting a hammer while you slept!’
pages.alt: Bra Yao grins in amazement as Afia shows the three-step staircase of compound growth from 1,000 to 1,100 to 1,210 to 1,331 cedis.

pages.text: Then Auntie Akua held up a warning finger. ‘Never forget that compound interest works in reverse when you borrow money!’ she cautioned. ‘If someone takes a high-interest loan and fails to pay on time, the unpaid interest is added to the debt, and next month they are charged interest on the unpaid interest too! Compounding is a wonderful servant for a saver, but a dangerous master for a careless borrower.’
sentences: Then Auntie Akua held up a warning finger.
‘Never forget that compound interest works in reverse when you borrow money!’ she cautioned.
‘If someone takes a high-interest loan and fails to pay on time, the unpaid interest is added to the debt, and next month they are charged interest on the unpaid interest too!
Compounding is a wonderful servant for a saver, but a dangerous master for a careless borrower.’
pages.alt: Auntie Akua illustrates how an unpaid high-interest debt snowballs larger and heavier down a hill.

pages.text: Suddenly Bra Yao pulled out his phone. ‘Wait, Auntie! A stranger in a group chat sent me a link called MegaFast Gold Doubler. It promises: Send 1,000 cedis today and receive 2,000 cedis guaranteed in just seven days, a 100 percent return in one week! Should I put my money there instead of a 10-percent annual bond or bank account?’
sentences: Suddenly Bra Yao pulled out his phone.
‘Wait, Auntie!
A stranger in a group chat sent me a link called MegaFast Gold Doubler.
It promises: Send 1,000 cedis today and receive 2,000 cedis guaranteed in just seven days, a 100 percent return in one week!
Should I put my money there instead of a 10-percent annual bond or bank account?’
pages.alt: Bra Yao holds up his smartphone showing a flashy message with gold coin icons while Auntie Akua and Afia look alarmed.

pages.text: ‘Stop right there, Yao, that is a classic financial scam!’ Auntie Akua said firmly. ‘In real finance, higher potential returns always come with higher risk, and no legitimate business or stock-market investment can ever guarantee 100 percent profit in a week! Schemes that pay early members using cash taken from newer members are fraudulent Ponzi schemes, and they always collapse. Before entrusting money to any institution, check that it is licensed by the Bank of Ghana or the Securities and Exchange Commission!’
sentences: ‘Stop right there, Yao, that is a classic financial scam!’ Auntie Akua said firmly.
‘In real finance, higher potential returns always come with higher risk, and no legitimate business or stock-market investment can ever guarantee 100 percent profit in a week!
Schemes that pay early members using cash taken from newer members are fraudulent Ponzi schemes, and they always collapse.
Before entrusting money to any institution, check that it is licensed by the Bank of Ghana or the Securities and Exchange Commission!’
pages.alt: Auntie Akua shows Bra Yao and Afia how to verify licensed financial institutions and spot the red flags of a Ponzi pyramid.

pages.text: On Monday afternoon, after classes, Afia accompanied Bra Yao to the licensed community bank. Together they placed 200 cedis into an instant-access emergency savings account and 800 cedis into a regulated fixed-term treasury investment where it would earn steady compound interest for three years while Yao finished his apprenticeship.
sentences: On Monday afternoon, after classes, Afia accompanied Bra Yao to the licensed community bank.

Together they placed 200 cedis into an instant-access emergency savings account and 800 cedis into a regulated fixed-term treasury investment where it would earn steady compound interest for three years while Yao finished his apprenticeship.
pages.alt: At a clean licensed community bank counter, Bra Yao and Afia receive an official deposit receipt from a bank teller.

pages.text: That night, Afia wrote at the top of a fresh page: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? ‘Financial intelligence means earning honestly, saving consistently, letting compound interest work patiently over years, and never falling for greedy shortcuts,’ she told Bra Yao. What long-term goal would you save and plan for, and how can you help your family spot financial scams before anyone loses hard-earned money?

activities.question: Why does 1,000 cedis locked in a box under the bed lose purchasing power when inflation is 8% per year?
options: Prices rise over time while idle cash in the box earns 0% return
Because wooden boxes eat paper banknotes at night
Because inflation makes toolsets weigh less
activities.explanation: When general prices rise (inflation) and idle cash earns nothing, the same 1,000 cedis buys fewer goods next year.

activities.definition: Interest calculated on both the original principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods
distractors: Money hidden inside an unlabelled plastic bag
A fee paid to join an unlicensed chat group

activities.question: If 1,000 cedis earns 10% compound interest per year, what is the balance after 2 years and after 3 years?
options: 1,210 cedis after Year 2 and 1,331 cedis after Year 3
1,200 cedis after Year 2 and 1,300 cedis after Year 3

activities.question: What is the biggest warning sign that an online investment offer like "Double your money, 100% guaranteed in 7 days" is a scam?
options: It promises huge "zero-risk" profit and lacks BoG or SEC licensing
It encourages you to study mathematics in school
It asks you to keep an emergency fund at a licensed bank
activities.explanation: In real finance, higher returns carry higher risk and are never guaranteed; "guaranteed fast doubling" is a classic Ponzi fraud indicator.

activities.prompt: Order the steps of wise financial decision-making that Bra Yao and Afia followed.
items: Learn how inflation and compound interest affect savings over time.
Reject unlicensed "get-rich-quick" schemes promising guaranteed high returns.
Divide savings between an emergency fund and a regulated long-term investment.

activities.prompt: Why does building real wealth require patience and discipline rather than chasing quick shortcuts?

glossary.definition: The general increase in prices of goods and services over time, which reduces what each unit of currency can buy
The original sum of money saved, invested, or borrowed before interest is added
Growing by earning returns on both the original principal and previously earned interest
A fraudulent investment scam that pays early participants with money taken from new participants rather than real business profits
